summary: Companion to GMPLS signaling that defines the technology-specific information needed to use GMPLS with SONET and SDH networks. It was replaced by RFC 4606.

eli5.summary: A general instruction book for setting up network paths needs a special chapter for one kind of phone-company cable system. This is that chapter.

questions: how does gmpls work with tdm networks
subtitle: Technology-specific rules for setting up SONET and SDH network paths using GMPLS signaling.

tldr.problem: GMPLS extends MPLS to support new interface types including time-division multiplex (TDM) networks like SONET and SDH, but each technology has specific signaling requirements.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines traffic parameters and label formats for SONET/SDH networks within GMPLS, including signal types, concatenation options, transparency requirements, and a hierarchical labeling scheme (SUKLM).
tldr.outcome: GMPLS can now control label-switched paths in SONET and SDH optical networks alongside packet networks. It was later superseded by RFC 4606 with updates.

facts.value: 12 types from VT1.5 SPE to STS-768/STM-256

today: RFC 3946 provided GMPLS signaling extensions for SONET and SDH networks. It was later superseded by RFC 4606, which updated and refined the SONET/SDH control extensions for GMPLS.

sections.title: GMPLS and Time-Division Multiplex
sections.content:
Generalized MPLS (GMPLS), defined in RFC 3945, extends the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) framework from packet-switched networks to include four new classes of interfaces and switching: Layer-2 Switch Capable (L2SC), Time-Division Multiplex (TDM), Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) for wavelength routing, and Fiber-Switch Capable (FSC). This RFC focuses on the TDM class, specifically SONET (Synchronous Optical Network, the North American standard) and SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy, the international standard for telecom networks).

SONET and SDH networks arrange data into structured time-slots within multiplexed signals. For GMPLS to establish label-switched paths (LSPs) in these networks, it must speak their language: understand their signal types, multiplexing hierarchies, concatenation rules, and transparency requirements. This document provides those technology-specific details, defining how GMPLS traffic parameters and labels map to SONET/SDH concepts.
sections.eli5: GMPLS is like a universal language for setting up paths across different types of networks. Telephone company cables speak SONET/SDH, which is a special dialect. This document teaches GMPLS how to talk SONET/SDH.

sections.title: Traffic Parameters for SONET/SDH
sections.content:
SONET and SDH traffic parameters define what kind of signals a path must carry. The parameters include a Signal Type (indicating whether the signal is a VT1.5, STS-1, STS-3c, or a full STS-N/STM-N frame), and four optional transforms that can be applied to the base signal. These transforms are: Requested Contiguous Concatenation (RCC), which bonds identical signals together; Number of Virtual Components (NVC), which groups signals with individual time-slot assignments; Transparency flags, which specify that frame overhead fields must pass through unchanged; and Multiplier (MT), which requests multiple identical signals in a single LSP.

Each transform must be applied in a strict order. For example, a path might request three STS-1 SPEs concatenated contiguously into a single STS-3c SPE, then multiplied by two to get two such concatenated signals. The Transparency field allows GMPLS to request that intermediate nodes preserve the SONET Section/Regenerator Section layer or the Line/Multiplex Section layer overhead without modification, important for carrying management data or preserving timing information across the network.
sections.eli5: Traffic parameters are a recipe that says 'I need X SPEs bunched together, Y sets of distributed signals, all my frame labels preserved, and Z copies of this setup.' Each ingredient is mixed in a specific order.

sections.title: Signal Types and Multiplexing Hierarchy
sections.content:
SONET and SDH define a hierarchy of signal types: the smallest is VT1.5 SPE (SONET) or VC-11 (SDH), which can be grouped into larger containers. The RFC lists twelve signal types ranging from the smallest virtual tributaries (VT1.5 through VT6) up to the largest frame signals (STS-192/STM-64). Each signal type represents a specific bit rate and a position in the multiplexing tree. A SONET STS-N signal, for example, contains three groups of identical units called STS-1s, and the position of a signal within this hierarchy determines its label.

The RFC notes that when requesting a SONET STS-Nc SPE where N is a multiple of three (e.g., STS-3, STS-9), the GMPLS request must use the STS-3c SPE signal type rather than representing it as individual STS-1 SPEs concatenated. This design choice facilitates interworking between SONET and SDH, since SDH's VC-4 directly corresponds to STS-3c SPE.
sections.eli5: SONET and SDH are like Russian nesting dolls. Tiny signals fit inside medium signals, which fit inside larger signals. This section says which dolls exist and how many fit inside each other.

sections.title: SONET/SDH Label Format and Multiplexing Trees
sections.content:
SONET and SDH labels in GMPLS use a five-field format called SUKLM, based on the G.707 standard. Each field identifies a branch in the multiplexing tree. The S field (1 to N) identifies which STS-3/AUG within an STS-N/STM-N multiplex; U field (1 to 3) identifies which STS-1/VC-3 within an STS-3/AUG; K field (1 to 3) identifies which TUG-3 within a VC-4; L field (1 to 7) identifies which VT Group/TUG-2 within an STS-1/VC-3; and M field identifies a specific tributary (VT1.5, VT2, VT3, or VT6) within a VT Group. A zero in any field means that field is not significant in the context, reducing the hierarchy for lower-order paths.

In case of contiguous concatenation, a single label identifies the lowest time-slot occupied by the concatenated signal. For virtual concatenation, an explicit ordered list of labels is given, with each label indicating the first time-slot of a virtually concatenated component. For multiplication (requesting multiple identical signals), all labels that form the final signal are listed in order.
sections.eli5: The label is like an address in a postal system. S says which city, U says which neighborhood, K says which street, L says which block, and M says which house. If you do not need all parts of the address, you use zeros for the parts that do not matter.

sections.title: Protocol Details for RSVP-TE and CR-LDP
sections.content:
GMPLS uses two signaling protocols: RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol - Traffic Engineering) and CR-LDP (Constraint-based LDP). This RFC defines how SONET/SDH traffic parameters and labels are encoded in each protocol. For RSVP-TE, traffic parameters are carried in SENDER_TSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects with specific class and type values (Class 12, C-Type 4 for SONET/SDH). For CR-LDP, they are carried in a SONET/SDH Traffic Parameters TLV with type 0x0838.

Both protocols perform validation at each hop: nodes check whether they support the requested Signal Type, concatenation options, virtual components, multiplier value, and transparency flags. If any requested parameter cannot be supported, the node generates an error message (PathErr for RSVP-TE, NOTIFICATION for CR-LDP) and rejects the LSP request. This ensures that all nodes along the path agree on what the path will carry.
sections.eli5: When a node receives a request to set up a path, it checks a checklist: 'Do I support this signal type? Can my cables handle this transparency? Is this multiplier valid?' If any answer is 'no,' it sends back an error message.
